blocks.text: The most important non-specific defence is given by the germ-killer cells of the blood, which patrol the bloodstream and attack and kill microbes. There are three basic kinds: macrophages, neutrophils and natural killer cells.

items: Macrophages develop from monocytes, a type of white blood cell. A macrophage takes in a bacterium by endocytosis and kills it with its enzymes. Some are fixed in organs such as the lungs, liver, spleen and brain, but most patrol the blood, lymph and interstitial fluid.

Neutrophils, another type of white blood cell, kill pathogens in three ways: phagocytosis; releasing soluble anti-microbial chemicals onto pathogens; and releasing a network of DNA fibres that binds and kills pathogenic bacteria.

blocks.alt: Left: a large macrophage with a pseudopod reaching towards bacteria, one bacterium already inside a vacuole surrounded by small lysosomes. Right: a neutrophil with a lobed nucleus shown three times: engulfing a bacterium, releasing orange chemical dots at a bacterium, and throwing out a net of purple DNA fibres that holds bacteria.
blocks.caption: Macrophages and neutrophils at work (original diagram after Figures 21.4 and 21.5).
blocks.long_description: Macrophages develop from monocytes. A macrophage takes in a bacterium by endocytosis and digests it with lysosomal enzymes; some macrophages are fixed in organs such as the lungs, liver, spleen and brain, while most patrol the blood, lymph and tissue fluid. Neutrophils kill in three ways: by phagocytosis, by releasing soluble anti-microbial chemicals onto pathogens, and by releasing a network of DNA fibres that binds and kills bacteria.

blocks.text: Natural killer (NK) cells do not kill invading microbes; they detect and attack body cells infected with viruses. They release perforins, which insert into the target cell's membrane and form a pore; water rushes in and the cell swells and bursts. They also detect cancer cells and kill them before they can develop into a tumour.

blocks.alt: A natural killer cell on the left releases purple perforin molecules towards a virus-infected cell on the right. Perforins sit as small square pores in the infected cell's membrane, and a blue arrow shows water rushing in through them.
blocks.caption: A natural killer cell and an infected cell (original diagram after Figure 21.6).
blocks.long_description: Natural killer cells do not kill invading microbes directly; they detect and attack body cells infected with viruses. They release perforins, proteins that insert into the target cell's membrane and form pores; water rushes in and the cell swells and bursts. NK cells can also detect cancer cells and kill them before they develop into a tumour.

blocks.title: Natural killer cells
blocks.text: Natural killer cells are a type of T-lymphocyte and are also called cytotoxic T cells.

blocks.title: For information: self-proteins
blocks.text: Patrolling cells do not attack the body's own cells, because all normal cells carry a surface protein marker that identifies them, the self-protein. Germ-killer cells attack only cells that lack such proteins.
